primitives.assumptions: Two-person officiating system assumes non-overlapping responsibilities: referee tracks ball, umpire enforces rules.

primitives.name: Player Position Hierarchy
primitives.verbatim_quote: There are two general divisions of players—the "rushers " or "forwards," so called because they constitute the front rank of the foot-ball army; and the backs, called the quarter-back, the half-back or halves, and the full-back or goal-tend.
primitives.assumptions: Players are partitioned into hierarchical roles based on spatial positioning and functional duties.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Role ambiguity or positional overlap leads to strategic inefficiency.

layer2.mapping: Hierarchical player roles form a kernel of tactical state space; rushers define attack frontier, backs define defense and support.
layer2.telemetry: Tactical success metrics per positional group.

The emergence of the referee-umpire duality reflects a foundational design principle in early American football: separation of duties to enhance system robustness. The referee focuses on ball tracking, while the umpire ensures compliance with rules. This dualism enables scalable governance of complex interactions. The player hierarchy introduces a structured division of labor: rushers engage in direct confrontation, while backs execute strategic maneuvers. These roles are not merely descriptive but operational, forming a kernel of tactical behavior. The evolution from 'forwards' to 'rushers' and 'goal-tends' to 'backs' indicates a linguistic shift toward more intuitive terminology, yet the underlying functional structure remains consistent. The adoption of dual umpires signals institutional adaptation to increasing game complexity, mirroring how modern systems scale control mechanisms. The failure mode of this system lies in lack of coordination or authority delegation, which can lead to rule ambiguities or enforcement gaps. Thus, the primitives encapsulate both the static structure of roles and the dynamic interplay of enforcement and strategy.
